summary: Discovery call with Halo Defense exploring Redwood Private (on-prem, air-gapped) deployment. transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-17
Start: 14:00 PT
Duration: 52 mins
Attendees: Michael Chen (Redwood AE), Sara Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Alvarez (Redwood SE), Tom Hargreaves (Halo CTO), Maya Singh (Halo Head of Cloud), Dr. Eric Lowe (Halo VP Security), Aisha Rahman (Halo Lead DevOps), Ben Carter (Procurement)

Summary (auto): Halo Defense is evaluating an on-prem, air-gapped deployment for Redwood Private. Primary drivers: strict export control, classified processing lanes, and regulatory auditability. Key concerns: how updates are delivered offline, attestations/signing of artifacts, allowed hardware (we have older cards and some new A100s), and proof of throughput/latency under constrained networking.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Michael Chen: Hey everyone, this is Michael from Redwood, thanks for taking the time. we've got sara and jordan with me; we'll do a quick agenda, dig into your constraints, and sara will go over the technical model and update flow.
[00:00:12] Tom Hargreaves: Hi Michael, thanks. I'll let maya and eric intro then we can jump in.
[00:00:20] Maya Singh: Hey all, Maya here. We're looking at options for running LLM inference in our classified lanes, so air-gapped, no direct internet. Need to understand operational model and how you do offline updates.
[00:00:33] Dr. Eric Lowe: Eric Lowe: from security, big focus on cryptographic signing, HSM integration, FIPS validated paths, and audit trails. We can't have model weights leaving the site.
[00:00:00] Michael Chen: Got it. that's helpful context. quick question on current infra  what GPUs do you have in your data center?
[00:00:48] Aisha Rahman: We have a mixed fleet. Majority are NVIDIA A100 40GB, some older V100s, and a couple of Ampere Ampere L40s in a test rack. Our network is backbone 10GbE with NVLink within racks, but cross-rack NVLink not available.
[00:01:05] Jordan Alvarez: OK, thanks. For model performance, NVLink within the node is good; cross-node model parallelism will be more limited without RDMA/InfiniBand. Is that accurate?
[00:01:20] Aisha Rahman: Yes, we don't have InfiniBand in the classified racks right now. 10GbE, some RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) is planned but not enabled in air-gapped zone.
[00:01:33] Sara Patel: Quick note  Redwood Private supports multiple topologies. For heavier model parallelism we can do sharded serving across nodes but it impacts latency. Alternatively quantized single-node variants often fit A100-40GB for many 70-13B style models.
[00:01:47] Tom Hargreaves: We're trying to avoid large model parallel setups; prefer simpler ops. What does your offline update process look like? How do we get patches and models to the air-gapped rack?
[00:02:02] Michael Chen: Good question. Our standard for Private air-gapped customers is a signed artifact approach. We produce a deployment bundle  container images, model weights (if applicable), and a signed manifest. The bundle can be delivered via encrypted USB or via an approved transfer node. We also provide checksums and signatures so your team can validate.
[00:02:22] Dr. Eric Lowe: We need the signing to be compatible with our HSM. Can we bring our own signing keys or use a customer-managed KMS/HSM?
[00:02:30] Sara Patel: Yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed keys. We integrate with HSMs for artifact signing and for in-cluster encryption keys. We also provide an offline attestation tool that runs locally to validate signatures against a public certificate you have.
[00:02:45] Maya Singh: How often do updates ship? We want a predictable patch cadence and an option to opt-out of automatic model changes.
[00:02:53] Michael Chen: For air-gapped, updates are scheduled  monthly security patches, model variant updates as agreed. Customers can approve each release. For pilot we'll propose a controlled window and you can opt into model changes only after validation.
[00:03:05] Aisha Rahman: What about telemetry? We can't send usage data offsite.
[00:03:09] Jordan Alvarez: By default we can disable telemetry. We also have on-prem observability modules that store logs and metrics in your cluster; if you want aggregated telemetry to Redwood it's opt-in and can be delivered via your secure transfer process.
[00:03:22] Dr. Eric Lowe: Audit logs we need immutable audit trails for inference requests and admin actions, retention 7 years. Do you offer WORM-style logs or a way to export signed logs?
[00:03:34] Sara Patel: We support append-only audit logs and can integrate with your SIEM. For long retention we can configure log forwarding to your immutable storage (offline tape or air-gapped object store). We can also produce signed log exports for periodic review.
[00:03:49] Tom Hargreaves: Great. Now, on the model side: licensing. We need to keep model weights on premises and must ensure no external calls to external models.
[00:03:58] Michael Chen: Redwood Private can run fully offline; model weights never leave your cluster once provisioned. We support both Redwood-curated open models and customer-provided proprietary models. For curated models we provide a signed weights bundle. For proprietary models we load from your artifact store.
[00:04:15] Maya Singh: Are there restrictions on some model architectures? For instance, our analytics workload prefers a smaller quantized 13B for low latency.
[00:04:24] Sara Patel: We commonly recommend quantization for cost and latency. We have quant profiles for multiple architectures. For 13B models on A100-40GB we can often run a quantized bf16/4-bit variant. We'll share recommended configs in the BOM.
[00:04:39] Aisha Rahman: Ok, on hardware BOM: besides GPUs, what about storage and NVMe? We have a 1U host with local NVMe but no shared storage in the rack.
[00:04:48] Jordan Alvarez: Local NVMe per node is fine. For large models we stream shards from local NVMe; we recommend at least 1TB NVMe per GPU for some larger families. If you want to avoid swapping you'd provision more.
[00:05:01] Tom Hargreaves: Networking: if we enable RoCE in the future, would Redwood take advantage of that?
[00:05:08] Sara Patel: Yes, with RDMA/InfiniBand we can enable more efficient kernel paths and better multi-node scaling. Without it we lean towards single-node quantized variants to keep latency down.
[00:05:19] Ben Carter: From procurement  rough cost range for pilot and then for 3-month reserved capacity?
[00:05:26] Michael Chen: We'll put numbers in the SOW; ballpark for a pilot (3 racks, software + support) we can provide a range. For reserved capacity we have monthly commits and options for hardware credits if you want Redwood to supply dedicated hardware. We'll include both customer-supplied and Redwood-supplied BOM pricing.
[00:05:43] Dr. Eric Lowe: Vulnerability scanning  do you run SBOM and image scanning before we accept bundles?
[00:05:49] Jordan Alvarez: Yes, we provide SBOMs for the images and we scan builds for CVEs. The signed bundle contains a vulnerability report; you can run your own scanners as well before importing.
[00:06:02] Maya Singh: Let's walk through a potential update flow so we're clear.
[00:06:06] Michael Chen: Sure. Step 1: Redwood produces signed bundle and SBOM. Step 2: Bundle is transferred via approved medium to Halo transfer node. Step 3: Local attestation tool verifies signatures against customer certs/HSM. Step 4: Staged deployment in a test rack. Step 5: Operator validation, smoke tests. Step 6: Approve and promote to production racks. All steps produce signed audit entries.
[00:06:30] Dr. Eric Lowe: That matches our compliance needs. Who has access to those private keys on Redwood side?
[00:06:36] Sara Patel: For image signing we can sign from Redwood with our CI keys; however for air-gapped customers we strongly recommend using your own key in your HSM to re-sign or to verify. We can support bring-your-own-key workflows.
[00:06:49] Aisha Rahman: What about emergency patches? If there's a zero-day we can't accept an unvetted bundle; is there an expedited process?
[00:06:57] Michael Chen: We can do an expedited release channel where we provide the patch bundle, and your security team can run a prioritized validation flow. We also provide a rollback mechanism and signed rollback artifacts.
[00:07:10] Tom Hargreaves: Any limitations with private repo or package dependencies when building images? We have strict internal registries.
[00:07:18] Jordan Alvarez: Redwood's build process can be reproduced in your environment. We provide Dockerfile and build artifacts so you can build images locally against your internal registry and sign them.
[00:07:30] Maya Singh: Latency expectations  for a quantized 13B on A100-40GB what's realistic 95th percentile for single-turn responses, say 256 tokens?
[00:07:40] Sara Patel: Ballpark: 100-180ms per token for autoregressive sampling is not uncommon, but it heavily depends on batch size and sampling strategy. We'll run your prompt sets in bench tests and provide p95 numbers.
[00:07:53] Tom Hargreaves: We also need token-level billing visibility and per-route quotas.
[00:07:58] Michael Chen: Redwood Console supports per-route metering and token-level cost/latency breakdowns. In private deployment we can enable the console components in-cluster; aggregated billing exports can be delivered via the secure transfer process.
[00:08:12] Ben Carter: What about SSO / SAML for admin access?
[00:08:16] Sara Patel: We support SAML/SSO, RBAC, and can integrate with your IdP. For air-gapped, SSO assertions are validated via local IdP or via a token exchange mechanism depends on your IdP topology.
[00:08:29] Dr. Eric Lowe: Data residency and telemetry  confirm nothing leaves site by default.
[00:08:34] Michael Chen: Correct. By default nothing leaves. Any telemetry or logs that you permit to leave are explicitly configured and transferred via your process.
[00:08:43] Maya Singh: We have one more question on model provenance. We need a chain-of-custody for model weights. Is that available?
[00:08:52] Jordan Alvarez: Yes, signed manifests and provenance metadata come with each bundle; they include origin, training data lineage notes if available for curated models, and a hash chain.
[00:09:05] Tom Hargreaves: Perfect. From here what's a reasonable pilot scope?
[00:09:10] Michael Chen: Pilot we propose: 2 racks, one test rack and one production-sim rack, 3 months. We'll run benchmark suite with your prompts, validate latency, throughput, and cold-start behavior. We'll also validate offline update flow. We'll provide a small team of SE hours for onboarding.
[00:09:27] Maya Singh: That sounds reasonable. Procurement timeline is end of Q2 for budget.
[00:09:33] Ben Carter: We'll need detailed SOW and pricing.
[00:09:36] Michael Chen: We'll get that over. I'll include both an option where you bring your own hardware and another where Redwood supplies dedicated hardware.
[00:09:45] Dr. Eric Lowe: One last item  regulatory attestations. We may need Redwood to submit to a security review and accommodate on-site audits (or remote review of artifacts).
[00:09:55] Sara Patel: We support audit processes. For air-gapped we can provide the artifacts and allow an on-site assessment with redacted operational data as agreed in NDA.
[00:10:05] Tom Hargreaves: Great. Any final questions?
[00:10:09] Maya Singh: No, good coverage.
[00:10:11] Michael Chen: OK I'll recap next steps. We'll send the security pack (SOC2, ISO artifacts), sample BOM and recommended config, and a pilot SOW. Sara will prepare a benchmark plan and Jordan will include SBOM and build reproducibility notes. We'll also schedule a technical deep dive with Aisha next week.
[00:10:28] Aisha Rahman: Sounds good. We'll share rack specs and the airgap transfer procedures.
[00:10:32] Ben Carter: I'll follow up on procurement dates.
[00:10:35] Michael Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with the docs and calendar invites.
[00:10:40] (crosstalk)
[00:10:44] End call

Notes about transcription: occasional mis-heard acronyms (e.g., 'K V cache' for 'KV cache') and punctuation artifacts. Occasional speaker label jitter where the SE remarks were attributed to the AE.
